description: We’re building a NASA Space Apps team to turn open space data into impactful, human-centered web solutions. I bring Python, SQL, React, and UI/UX design (Figma) to connect data with clean visuals. Looking for teammates in Earth/space science, geospatial analysis, 3D/data viz, or storytelling/pitching. If you want to build a polished, creative project together, request to join!
summary:
Earth-based flammability standards create a dangerous false sense of security in microgravity, where materials certified on Earth can sustain persistent combustion under cabin airflow.

While decades of microgravity combustion tests exist in NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database, the data is vast and difficult to navigate.

To directly address NASA’s Flame in Freefall challenge, our team created PYROIS, an interactive, web-based Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) Flight Safety Console. Grounded in experimental flight records from NASA's microgravity investigations, our tool executes three core functions: 

- Summarizes: Harmonizes historical microgravity combustion test archives into normalized physical telemetry across pressurized habitat sectors.
- Ranks: Evaluates material flammability and ignition probabilities across non-linear oxygen and airflow envelopes, modeling the microgravity "Airflow Paradox" with statistical uncertainty bounds.
- Interprets: Exposes root-cause flammability discrepancies between terrestrial standards and spaceflight, delivering docked qualification audits and deterministic NASA-STD-6001B mitigation directives.

PYROIS bridges the gap between historical combustion science and real-time habitat safety to deliver actionable operational insights for safer exploration.
details:
System Architecture and Operational Workflow

PYROIS (Pyrotechnic and Flammability Operational Intelligence System) functions as an interactive Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) Flight Safety Console. It bridges the gap between historical microgravity combustion research and live spacecraft habitat operations through an end-to-end data and modeling pipeline:

  • Environmental Telemetry Normalization: Cabin atmospheric parameters are dynamically routed across pressurized habitat compartments, including the Crew Quarters, Avionics Equipment Bay, and Microgravity Glovebox Bay. Telemetry dials track total pressure (P in kPa), oxygen concentration (%O2), forced ventilation velocity (V in cm/s), and localized gravity (g).
    • Gaussian Process Regressor: Maps flame spread velocity across ventilation regimes, generating the nonlinear "Airflow Paradox" response alongside continuous ±2σ uncertainty halos to quantify sparse flight data risks.
    • Polynomial Logistic Regression: Models non-linear O2% × Airflow flammability boundaries to evaluate continuous ignition probabilities across materials.
    • Random Forest Classifier: Evaluates multi-sensor telemetry to classify cabin states into operational tiers: Nominal, Drift Warning, Smoldering Risk, and Active Suppression.
  • Material Ranking and Qualification Audits: The console ranks candidate aerospace materials (including PMMA Cast Acrylic, Kapton HN, Silicone RTV-560, and Nomex HT90-40) on a live Leaderboard. Selecting any material opens a docked Material Qualification Audit Drawer, linking active compartment physics against NASA-STD-6001B certification standards and providing deterministic mitigation steps such as ventilation throttling or O2 scrubbing thresholds.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Architecture

  • Frontend Application: Built with React and TypeScript, bundled with Vite, and styled with Tailwind CSS for a modular, high-density aerospace HUD interface.
  • Custom Interactive Instruments: Rotary dials are implemented as custom React SVG components with custom event listeners supporting mouse drag, touch gestures, and keyboard stepping.
  • Data Visualizations: Built using Recharts to render the dynamic Airflow Paradox flame spread curve, statistical ±2σ uncertainty bands, and reference markers for quench, low-flow peak, and blow-off limits.
  • Backend API and ML Runtime: Python with FastAPI, served asynchronously by Uvicorn, hosting the scikit-learn models and data ingestion services.
  • NASA Data Sources and Flight Standards: Microgravity combustion databases include NASA BASS (PSI-26), BASSII (PSI-25), Saffire-I (PSI-98), Saffire-II(PSI-99), Saffire-III(PSI-100), and FLEX (PSI-69). Flight certification standards include NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 upward flame propagation records and NASA-STD-3001 human spaceflight habitability and environmental standards.

Operational Benefits and Intended Impact

Current spacecraft fire safety relies heavily on terrestrial 1g testing (NASA-STD-6001B Test 1). On Earth, natural buoyant convection draws cool air into the flame base and carries heat upward, often blowing out or self-extinguishing materials. In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy removes this convective cooling. Under forced spacecraft cabin ventilation (1 to 20 cm/s), materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth can sustain persistent combustion, creating the dangerous "False-Pass" dilemma.

PYROIS provides immediate operational impact:

  • Pre-Mission Material Screening: Enables ECLSS engineers designing lunar and Martian habitats to qualify materials under exploration atmospheres (such as 56 kPa with 34% O2 for lunar EVA pre-breathe) rather than sea-level Earth air.
  • In-Flight Decision Support: Equips flight safety officers with proactive mitigation protocols (such as precise airflow cutoff speeds) before an anomaly transitions from smoldering to open fire.

Creative Engineering and Innovation

  • Visualizing the Airflow Paradox: Rather than treating flammability as a binary pass/fail score, PYROIS visually illustrates the microgravity airflow curve, highlighting how zero flow starves a flame of oxygen (quench), lowspeed flow accelerates flame spread, and high flow blows it out.
  • Honest Uncertainty Halos: Acknowledging the inherent sparsity of spaceflight combustion data, the system visualizes the Gaussian Process 2σ uncertainty band, showing operators exactly where empirical predictions are confident versus where test data is scarce.
  • Docked Qualification Audit: Closes the loop between predictive machine learning and regulatory engineering by mapping model outputs directly back to NASA-STD-6001B protocols and historical PSI flight test IDs.

Engineering Factors and Constraints Considered

  • Atmospheric Variability: The architecture accounts for the wide environmental envelopes of current and future missions, from nominal ISS operations (101.3 kPa, 21% O2) to Artemis Exploration Atmospheres (56.0 kPa, 34% O2) and pure oxygen spacesuit purges.
  • Microgravity Smoldering Physics: Addressed low-flow zones behind avionics equipment racks (less than 5 cm/s), where the lack of convection leads to localized heat accumulation and sustained low-temperature smolder.
  • Model Selection for Small Datasets: Recognizing that spaceflight combustion archives consist of hundreds of test points rather than millions, the team avoided uninterpretable deep neural networks. Instead, Gaussian Processes and regularized regressions were selected to prevent overfitting and deliver reliable, physically grounded boundaries.
  • Algorithmic Domain Guardrails and Dual-Regime Logic: To maintain flight safety integrity and prevent machine learning hallucination, the console enforces strict domain-validity guardrails. When atmospheric presets fall outside dense NASA BASS-II flight training bounds, the system deliberately restricts solver previews and flags conditions as [Extrapolated] or Scenario Unavailable rather than predicting ungrounded physics. Furthermore, selecting an Earth 1.00g baseline automatically switches the console from microgravity airflow models to terrestrial NASA-STD-6001B Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) qualification tables, directly reflecting the physical transition where buoyant convection dominates.
